title: Backtracking
tagline: Systematically explore all candidate solutions by building them incrementally and abandoning ('pruning') any path that cannot lead to a valid answer.

sections.content:
There is a class of problems where no shortcut exists — you must explore a **combinatorial search space** and consider many possibilities before finding a solution. Examples include placing eight queens on a chessboard with no conflicts, solving a sudoku puzzle, generating every permutation of a word, or finding all paths through a maze. The naive approach — enumerate every possible candidate and check each one — is called brute force, and it is almost always catastrophically slow: for n=20 elements, the number of permutations exceeds a trillion.

**Backtracking** is a disciplined refinement of brute force. Instead of generating all candidates first and filtering them afterwards, it builds candidates **incrementally**, one choice at a time. After each choice, it immediately checks whether the partial candidate can possibly lead to a valid solution. If not — if a constraint is already violated — it **prunes** that entire branch of possibilities and **backtracks** to the previous decision point to try a different option. This way, enormous swaths of the search space are discarded without ever being explicitly enumerated.

The term 'backtracking' was coined by mathematician D.H. Lehmer in the 1950s, and the technique was systematically studied in the context of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) in the 1960s–70s. Today it appears in every corner of computing: compilers use it for parsing ambiguous grammars, AI uses it for constraint satisfaction, and competitive programming uses it for combinatorial search. Understanding backtracking deeply means understanding how to explore structured search spaces efficiently — a skill that transfers directly to graph traversal, dynamic programming, and even database query planning.

This chapter covers the universal backtracking template, how pruning works and why it matters, worked examples at increasing depth (permutations, subsets, N-Queens, sudoku, combination sum), common pitfalls in implementation, and the relationship between backtracking and other algorithm families.

sections.title: Navigating a Hedge Maze by Marking Dead Ends
sections.content:
Imagine you are dropped into the centre of a large hedge maze and asked to find every exit. A brute-force approach would be to mentally enumerate every conceivable path from start to finish — there are exponentially many. That is not how people actually solve mazes.

The natural human strategy is: walk forward, making choices at every junction. Keep a mental note of where you came from. If you reach a dead end — a wall or a passage you have already visited — **retrace your steps to the last junction** and try the next untried direction. Mark dead ends so you never re-enter them. Continue until you have tried all branches from every junction.

This is exactly backtracking. The 'junction' is a **choice point** — a node in the decision tree where multiple options exist. The 'dead end' is a **constraint violation** — a partial candidate that can never be completed into a solution. 'Marking dead ends' is **pruning** — permanently discarding entire subtrees. And 'retracing your steps' is the **backtrack** operation — undoing the last choice and restoring the state to what it was before that choice was made.

The critical observation is that when you mark a dead-end passage in a maze, you eliminate not just that single corridor but every path that passes through it. In a decision tree, pruning a node at depth k eliminates an entire subtree — potentially millions of candidates — with a single constraint check. That is the power of backtracking: intelligent pruning makes the effective search space orders of magnitude smaller than the worst-case theoretical space.

sections.title: The Universal Backtracking Template
sections.content:
Every backtracking algorithm follows the same three-step recursive structure, regardless of the specific problem. Internalising this template is the single most valuable thing you can do:

**Step 1 — Base cases.** At the top of the function, check two things: (a) Has the goal been reached? If yes, record the current candidate as a solution and return. (b) Is the current partial candidate already invalid? If yes, prune — return immediately without recursing further.

**Step 2 — Enumerate choices.** For each available choice at the current decision point, execute the choose-recurse-unchoose loop:
- **Choose**: make the choice — modify the shared state (add an element to a path, place a queen on the board, mark a cell as used).
- **Explore**: recurse on the next subproblem with one fewer decision to make.
- **Unchoose (backtrack)**: undo the choice — restore the shared state to exactly what it was before the choose step.

The **undo step is not optional**. Backtracking uses a **single shared mutable state** (one board, one path array, one used-set) rather than copying state at every level. If you fail to undo, the next sibling branch inherits corrupted state and produces wrong answers. This is the most common implementation bug for beginners.

The template in pseudocode is always:
```
function backtrack(state):
  if isGoal(state): record(state); return
  if isInvalid(state): return              // prune
  for each choice in availableChoices(state):
    makeChoice(state, choice)              // mutate
    backtrack(nextState)                   // recurse
    undoChoice(state, choice)              // restore
```

Notice that pruning can happen either at the **start of the recursive call** (check validity on entry) or **before the recursive call** (check validity before even making it). Pruning before the call is more efficient — it avoids the function-call overhead for invalid branches entirely. Both are correct; early pruning is faster.

flowchart TD
    A["backtrack(state)"] --> B{"isGoal?"}
    B -- yes --> C["record solution"]
    B -- no --> D{"isInvalid?"}
    D -- yes --> E["return — PRUNE"]
    D -- no --> F["for each choice"]
    F --> G["makeChoice"]
    G --> H["backtrack recursively"]
    H --> I["undoChoice"]
    I --> F
sections.caption: The universal backtracking control flow. Every backtracking algorithm is a specialisation of this structure — the only variation is what 'isGoal', 'isInvalid', and 'makeChoice/undoChoice' mean for the specific problem.

sections.title: Worked Example: Generating All Permutations
sections.content:
**Permutations** are a clean first example because the structure is simple and the undo step is obvious.

Given an array `[1, 2, 3]`, generate all six permutations. The decision tree has three levels: at level 0 choose which element goes in position 0; at level 1 choose which remaining element goes in position 1; at level 2 there is only one element left — place it.

State: a `path` array (the partial permutation being built) and a `used` boolean array (tracks which elements are already in `path`).

Goal condition: `path.length === nums.length` — all elements placed.

Constraint / pruning: skip any element where `used[i]` is true — it is already in `path`.

Choose: `used[i] = true; path.push(nums[i])`.

Unchoose: `used[i] = false; path.pop()`.

The decision tree at level 0 has 3 branches (any of the 3 elements). At level 1, 2 branches remain. At level 2, 1. Total leaves = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 = 3!. For duplicates, add a sort + skip-if-same-as-previous-unused pruning rule, which cuts the tree further.

**Why no pruning beyond 'already used'?** Because for plain permutations, any ordering of distinct elements is valid — there is no additional constraint to violate. All 6 leaves are solutions. When the problem adds constraints (e.g., 'no two adjacent elements can be equal'), the pruning becomes richer and the explored subtree shrinks.

sections.title: Worked Example: Subsets and the Power Set
sections.content:
**Subsets** (also called the power set problem) introduce a different branching structure. For each element, the choice is binary: **include it or exclude it**. The decision tree has depth n (one level per element) and branching factor exactly 2. With n=3 elements, the tree has 2^3 = 8 leaves — one per subset.

Because every leaf is a valid subset (there is no constraint that could be violated), there is no pruning — every path to a leaf is recorded. The `start` index is the key: at each recursive call, only elements at index `>= start` are considered, which both avoids duplicates and generates subsets in natural order without a `used` array.

For **combination sum** — find all subsets that sum to a target — the same structure applies, but now there is a real constraint to prune: if the running sum already exceeds the target, stop recursing. If the input is sorted in ascending order, this prune is efficient: exceeding the target on element `i` means element `i+1`, `i+2`, etc. would also exceed it, so the inner loop can `break` rather than just `continue`. This is a classic example of **ordering choices to maximise pruning**.

The subset-with-constraint pattern covers a huge family of interview problems: word break, palindrome partitioning, letter combinations of a phone number, restore IP addresses. All share the same tree structure; the only variation is the constraint check.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Three problems, one template. In permutations, the 'used' array is the state that is chosen/unchosen. In subsets, the 'start' index replaces 'used' — it ensures each element is considered only once and in order. In combinationSum, the constraint check `candidates[i] > remaining` followed by `break` (not continue) is the key pruning insight — sorting makes the break valid because all subsequent candidates are also too large.

sections.title: Deep Dive: N-Queens — Constraint Engineering
sections.content:
**N-Queens** is the canonical backtracking benchmark. Place n queens on an n×n chessboard such that no two queens share a row, column, or diagonal. For n=8 the brute-force search space is 8^8 ≈ 16.7 million placements; backtracking with good constraint encoding explores only ~15,720 nodes — a 1000x reduction.

**One queen per row** — by design, we place exactly one queen per row, iterating row by row. This eliminates the row constraint entirely: each recursive call handles exactly one row, so two queens can never share a row.

**Column and diagonal constraints** need active tracking. A queen at (row, col) attacks:
- The entire column `col` — tracked in a `Set` called `cols`.
- The `\` diagonal: all cells where `row - col` is the same constant — tracked in `Set diag1`.
- The `/` diagonal: all cells where `row + col` is the same constant — tracked in `Set diag2`.

Checking any of these three constraints is O(1) (hash set lookup), versus O(n) if you scanned the board. This encoding is the key to efficient N-Queens implementation.

**Pruning in action**: For n=4, the first row has 4 column choices. After placing a queen in column 0 of row 0, column 0, the `\` diagonal `0-0=0`, and the `/` diagonal `0+0=0` are all marked. In row 1, columns 0 (col conflict), 1 (`/` diagonal 1+0=1 is free, but `\` diagonal 1-1=0 conflicts), and 2 are candidates. In column 1: `cols` does not contain 1, `diag1` contains 0 (row 1 - col 1 = 0, conflict). Skip. Column 2: `cols` does not contain 2, `diag1` does not contain -1 (1-2=-1), `diag2` does not contain 3 (1+2=3). Valid — place here.

This incremental checking, applied before every recursive call, means entire subtrees are skipped. For n=8, of the 8 choices at row 0, only 6 survive into row 1 (two are immediately pruned). The tree narrows dramatically at each level due to the accumulating diagonal constraints.

**Counting vs. finding**: If you only need to count solutions (not enumerate boards), you can drop the board representation and just count. For n=8 there are exactly **92 solutions**; of these, 12 are fundamentally distinct (the rest are rotations and reflections). For n=13 there are 73,712 solutions — still found quickly by backtracking but impossible to enumerate by brute force in any reasonable time.

Using `row - col` as a key for the backslash diagonal and `row + col` for the forward slash diagonal is a standard trick: these values are unique per diagonal across the entire board, so O(1) conflict detection replaces O(n) scanning. The count-only variant drops board reconstruction, halving memory use.

sections.title: Advanced: Sudoku and Constraint Propagation
sections.content:
**Sudoku** pushes backtracking to its practical limit and introduces the idea of **constraint propagation** — using constraints not just to prune during search, but to reduce the search space before recursing.

A standard 9×9 sudoku has 81 cells. Empty cells must be filled with digits 1–9 such that no digit repeats in any row, column, or 3×3 box. Pure backtracking fills cells left-to-right, top-to-bottom: for each empty cell, try digits 1–9, check validity, recurse, undo. This works but is slower than necessary.

**Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) heuristic**: Instead of filling cells in order, always choose the **most constrained** empty cell — the one with the fewest valid digits. A cell with only one valid digit is forced (commit immediately for free). A cell with only two valid digits fails 50% of the time at the next level, pruning high in the tree. Contrast with a cell that has 7 valid digits — failing there prunes very little. MRV ensures that failures are detected as early and as high in the tree as possible, maximising the subtrees eliminated per backtrack.

**Constraint propagation (AC-3 / naked singles)**: After placing a digit in a cell, immediately eliminate that digit from the domains (valid-digit sets) of all 20 peers (8 in the same row, 8 in the same column, 4 more in the same box not already counted). If any peer's domain collapses to a single value, fill it and propagate again. This cascades — a single placement can fill dozens of cells without any backtracking. This is not guessing; it is deduction. Combined with MRV, sudoku backtracking solves every published puzzle almost instantly, often with zero actual backtracking needed.

**Why this matters beyond sudoku**: The combination of (1) incremental constraint checking, (2) MRV variable ordering, and (3) constraint propagation defines the state-of-the-art approach to **Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs)** in AI. The same ideas appear in scheduling, planning, configuration, and satisfiability (SAT) solvers. Backtracking is the algorithmic engine; constraint propagation is the intelligence layer on top of it.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Pick next cell\nMRV: fewest valid digits"] --> B["Try digit d"]
    B --> C{"Valid in row,\ncol, box?"}
    C -- no --> D["Try next digit"]
    C -- yes --> E["Place d\nPropagate constraints"]
    E --> F{"Any cell\ndomain empty?"}
    F -- yes --> G["Undo + backtrack"]
    F -- no --> H["Recurse on next\nmost-constrained cell"]
    H --> I{"All cells filled?"}
    I -- yes --> J["Solution found"]
    I -- no --> A
sections.caption: Sudoku solver flow: MRV cell selection + constraint propagation before recursing. If propagation reveals a contradiction (empty domain), backtrack immediately — no need to recurse further.

sections.title: Backtracking Complexity and Pruning Effectiveness
sections.content:
**Theoretical complexity** of backtracking is almost always exponential: O(n!) for permutations, O(2^n) for subsets, O(n!) for N-Queens. This is unavoidable — the output itself can have that many items. But theoretical worst-case complexity can be very misleading for backtracking because the **pruning effectiveness determines practical performance**.

For N-Queens with n=8, the theoretical bound is 8^8 ≈ 16.7 million. The actual nodes explored is ~15,720 — a factor of 1000 reduction. For n=12, theoretical 12^12 ≈ 8.9 billion; actual ~261,000 — a factor of 34,000 reduction. The ratio gets better as n grows because the constraint density increases.

For sudoku, the theoretical bound is 9^81 (try every digit for every empty cell) — a number so large it cannot be meaningfully printed. With constraint propagation and MRV, the practical search explores fewer than a hundred nodes for even hard puzzles.

**What determines pruning effectiveness?**
1. **Constraint tightness** — problems with many hard constraints prune more. A sudoku has 3 constraints per cell (row + col + box); N-Queens has 3 (col + 2 diagonals). Lightly constrained problems (e.g., find any path in a graph) prune little.
2. **Early placement of constrained choices** — MRV puts the hard choices first. Backtracking high in the tree (near the root) eliminates subtrees of maximum depth.
3. **Constraint propagation** — eliminating choices from future variables via constraint inference before recursing. This shrinks the branching factor at lower levels.
4. **Symmetry breaking** — many problems have symmetric solutions (e.g., N-Queens solutions related by reflection). Eliminating symmetric branches halves (or more) the search space.

**Memoization and backtracking**: Backtracking does not cache intermediate results — it explores each branch fresh. This contrasts with dynamic programming, which memoizes overlapping subproblems. If a backtracking problem has **overlapping subproblems** (the same partial state is reached via multiple paths), DP is usually the better tool. Pure backtracking is appropriate when the search space is a tree (no repeated subproblems) or when you need to enumerate all solutions rather than find one optimal one.

sections.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
sections.content:
**Forgetting to undo the choice (backtrack).** This is the most common bug. If you `push` to a path but forget to `pop`, or set `used[i] = true` but forget to set it back to `false`, every sibling branch after the first will see corrupted state. The fix is always to pair every mutation with its inverse: push/pop, add/delete, set true/set false. Write these as adjacent lines and make undoing impossible to forget.

**Copying state instead of undoing mutations.** Some implementations pass a copy of the state at every recursive call (`backtrack([...path, newItem])`) rather than mutating and undoing. This is correct but uses O(n·depth) memory and O(n) time for copying at every node — for large trees this is significantly slower. The mutation + undo pattern is preferred for performance. However, for immutable-style functional code, copying is cleaner and easier to reason about.

**Pruning too late.** Checking the constraint inside the recursive call (at the start of `backtrack(state)`) rather than before the call means one extra function call per invalid state. For problems with a large branching factor and tight constraints, moving the check before the call reduces overhead noticeably. LeetCode's time limits often require this optimisation.

**Wrong base case ordering.** The goal check and the prune check must both come before the loop over choices. If you loop first, you make choices from an already-invalid state. The correct order is: check goal, check invalid, then loop.

**Not handling duplicates in input.** For problems like 'subsets with duplicates' or 'permutations with duplicates', failing to sort the input and add a duplicate-skip condition (`if (i > start && nums[i] === nums[i-1]) continue`) produces repeated solutions in the output. Always ask: can the input contain duplicates? Do I need unique output?

**Using the wrong branching structure.** Permutations use a `used[]` array (any unused element can go in any position). Subsets use a `start` index (only elements after the current start are considered). Confusing these generates wrong or incomplete results. The deciding question: can any element appear in any position (permutation), or must elements be chosen in order (combination/subset)?

sections.title: Backtracking vs Related Algorithm Paradigms
sections.content:
**Backtracking vs. Brute Force**: Brute force generates all candidates and then tests each. Backtracking tests during construction and prunes early. Both are exhaustive in the worst case, but backtracking's early termination can be orders of magnitude faster in practice.

**Backtracking vs. Dynamic Programming**: DP is optimal when subproblems overlap and you need an optimal value (min/max count). Backtracking is right when you need to enumerate all solutions, when subproblems do not overlap, or when you need any valid solution to a constraint satisfaction problem. Some problems admit both: word break can be solved with backtracking (enumerate all ways) or DP (does any valid segmentation exist). The DP solution is usually O(n^2); the backtracking solution is exponential but tells you all segmentations.

**Backtracking vs. BFS/DFS on graphs**: DFS on an explicit graph avoids revisiting nodes via a `visited` set. Backtracking on an implicit decision tree avoids revisiting via constraint pruning and the undo step. The key difference: in graph DFS, the graph is fixed and nodes are discovered; in backtracking, the 'graph' (decision tree) is implicit and generated on the fly by choices. Backtracking is DFS on an implicit state space graph.

**Backtracking vs. Branch and Bound**: Branch and bound is backtracking augmented with a **bound function** — an estimate of the best possible solution reachable from a partial candidate. If the bound is worse than the best solution found so far, prune. This is used for optimisation problems (TSP, knapsack) where backtracking finds all solutions and branch-and-bound finds only the optimal one, pruning provably suboptimal branches.

Understanding these relationships helps you choose the right technique: if you need all solutions → backtracking; if you need the optimal value and subproblems overlap → DP; if you need the optimal solution in a large combinatorial space → branch and bound; if the space is an explicit graph → BFS (shortest path) or DFS (reachability).

**Historical context**: Backtracking's formal study began with D.H. Lehmer's 1950s work on combinatorial search. Donald Knuth's 1975 paper 'Estimating the efficiency of backtrack programs' introduced the technique of randomly sampling paths to **estimate** how large a backtracking tree is before running the full search — useful for deciding whether backtracking is feasible. Knuth also invented **Algorithm X** (implemented as Dancing Links / DLX) — an exact cover algorithm that solves sudoku and pentomino tiling via highly optimised backtracking with constraint propagation. The DPLL algorithm (1962) for propositional satisfiability (SAT) is essentially backtracking with unit propagation — and is the foundation of modern SAT solvers that can handle millions of variables.

**Interview and exam insight**: Backtracking problems on LeetCode/Codeforces follow a short list of patterns. (1) **Permutations / permutations with duplicates**: `used[]` array + optional duplicate-skip. (2) **Subsets / combinations**: `start` index + optional sum constraint. (3) **Board placement** (N-Queens, sudoku): constraint sets or arrays checked per choice. (4) **Path-building in a grid** (word search): in-place mark visited (`board[r][c] = '#'`) then unmark. Recognising which pattern applies is 80% of solving the problem. The undo step is always the mirror image of the choose step — if your choose is `path.push(x)`, undo is `path.pop()`. If your choose is `grid[r][c] = '#'`, undo is `grid[r][c] = originalChar`. Write them as a pair, never one without the other.

items: Backtracking is **constrained exhaustive search**: build the solution incrementally one choice at a time, immediately **prune** any partial candidate that violates a constraint, and **undo** each choice before trying the next sibling — the undo step is what makes the shared-state model correct across branches.

The **universal template** is: (1) if goal reached → record; (2) if state invalid → prune (return); (3) for each choice → choose → recurse → unchoose. Every backtracking algorithm is a specialisation of this structure.

**Pruning effectiveness determines practical performance**: N-Queens with n=8 has a theoretical space of 16.7M but backtracking explores only ~15,720 nodes (1000x reduction). The quality of constraint checks — O(1) set lookups for columns and diagonals — makes this possible.

**Three patterns cover most problems**: `used[]` array for permutations (any unused element, any position); `start` index for combinations/subsets (elements in order); constraint sets for board placement (queens, sudoku cells). Recognise the pattern before coding.

**MRV (minimum remaining values) heuristic** — choosing the most-constrained variable next — front-loads failures, maximising the subtrees eliminated per backtrack. Combined with constraint propagation (eliminating choices from future variables after each placement), it makes sudoku solvable with near-zero backtracking.

**Backtracking vs. DP**: use backtracking to enumerate all solutions or solve CSPs with no overlapping subproblems; use DP when subproblems overlap and you need an optimal value. Some problems (word break, coin change) admit both — DP finds whether a solution exists; backtracking finds all solutions.

The **most common bug** is forgetting the undo step — always write choose and unchoose as adjacent paired lines. The **most impactful optimisation** is moving the constraint check before the recursive call to avoid function-call overhead for invalid branches.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between backtracking and pure brute force?
options: Backtracking uses dynamic programming to cache partial results and avoid recomputation
Backtracking builds candidates incrementally and prunes any partial candidate the moment it violates a constraint, skipping entire subtrees
Backtracking always runs in polynomial time; brute force is exponential
Backtracking requires sorted input; brute force does not
quiz.explanation: Pure brute force enumerates all candidates upfront and filters at the end. Backtracking builds candidates one choice at a time and immediately abandons any partial candidate that violates a constraint — pruning entire subtrees without ever enumerating them. Both are exhaustive in the worst case, but backtracking's early termination can reduce explored states by orders of magnitude in practice.

quiz.question: In the backtracking template, what is the purpose of the 'unchoose' (undo) step?
options: It deletes the solution recorded in this branch to save memory
It restores shared mutable state to what it was before the current choice, so the next sibling branch sees a clean slate
It signals the recursion to terminate when no valid solutions remain
It re-sorts the available choices before trying the next option
quiz.explanation: Backtracking uses a single shared mutable state (one path array, one board, one used-set) across all recursive calls. Each call must restore whatever it mutated before returning — otherwise the next sibling branch inherits corrupted state and produces wrong answers. The undo step makes state changes reversible, enabling correct exploration of all branches from a clean starting point.

quiz.question: Why should the constraint check be placed BEFORE the recursive call rather than at the START of the recursive call?
options: Checking before the call allows memoization of pruned branches
Checking before the call avoids creating a stack frame for invalid branches, eliminating function-call overhead for pruned subtrees
Checking before the call converts the algorithm from exponential to polynomial
Checking at the start is always correct; before the call is only a style preference
quiz.explanation: If the constraint check is inside the recursive function, an invalid branch still incurs a function call before being rejected (stack frame allocation, argument passing). Placing the check before the call means no stack frame is created for invalid branches at all — the branch is pruned before entering. For algorithms with large branching factors and tight constraints, this can meaningfully reduce runtime.

quiz.question: In N-Queens, what three data structures are used to detect column and diagonal conflicts in O(1) per cell?
options: Three 2D arrays, one each for rows, columns, and diagonals
A hash set for columns, a hash set for backslash diagonals keyed on (row-col), and a hash set for forward-slash diagonals keyed on (row+col)
A single adjacency matrix representing all queen-attack relationships
A sorted array of occupied columns and two sorted arrays of diagonal offsets
quiz.explanation: A queen at (row, col) attacks its column, its backslash diagonal (where row-col is constant), and its forward-slash diagonal (where row+col is constant). Storing three hash sets keyed on col, (row-col), and (row+col) gives O(1) conflict detection. Scanning the board for conflicts would be O(n) per cell, making the overall algorithm significantly slower.

quiz.question: For generating subsets of an array using backtracking, why does the recursive call pass `i + 1` as the new `start` index?
options: To limit recursion depth and prevent stack overflow
To ensure each element is considered only once per subset and subsets are generated in order, avoiding duplicates like [1,2] and [2,1]
To skip elements that have already been pruned by a constraint check
To implement the minimum remaining values heuristic
quiz.explanation: Passing `start = i + 1` restricts subsequent elements to those with a higher index than the current one. This guarantees each unique subset is generated exactly once in lexicographic order. Without it, [1,2] and [2,1] would both appear (duplicate subsets), and elements could be used twice in the same subset.

quiz.question: In the combinationSum problem (subsets summing to a target), why does the inner loop use `break` instead of `continue` when a candidate exceeds the remaining sum?
options: break is a syntax requirement when the input is sorted
Because the candidates are sorted in ascending order, if candidates[i] exceeds the remaining sum, all subsequent candidates are also too large — break prunes all remaining iterations at once
break prevents integer overflow when remaining becomes negative
continue would cause an infinite loop because the start index is not incremented
quiz.explanation: When candidates are sorted ascending, once candidates[i] > remaining, candidates[i+1], candidates[i+2], etc. are also all > remaining. Using break exits the entire loop at that point, pruning all subsequent iterations without checking them. Using continue would only skip candidates[i] and still check the larger ones — a missed pruning opportunity.

quiz.question: What is the Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) heuristic in backtracking for constraint satisfaction problems?
options: Always try the smallest digit value first when filling a cell
Always choose the variable (e.g., empty cell) with the fewest valid assignments next, so failures are detected earliest and highest in the tree
Always process variables in the order they appear in the input
Reduce the domain of all variables to their minimum size before starting search
quiz.explanation: MRV selects the most-constrained unassigned variable next — the one with the fewest valid options. A variable with 1 valid value is forced (free commit). A variable with 2 valid values fails 50% of the time at the next level, pruning the tree high. Contrast with a variable that has 8 valid values — failing there prunes much less. MRV maximises the subtrees eliminated per backtrack by front-loading failures.

quiz.question: How many valid solutions does the 8-Queens problem have?
quiz.explanation: There are exactly 92 distinct solutions to the 8-Queens problem. Of these, 12 are fundamentally unique (the rest are rotations and reflections of those 12). The brute-force search space is 8^8 ≈ 16.7 million placements; backtracking with constraint encoding explores only ~15,720 nodes — roughly a 1000x reduction.

quiz.question: What is the most common implementation bug in backtracking algorithms?
options: Using a hash set instead of an array for constraint tracking
Checking the goal condition before the invalid condition
Forgetting to undo the choice (omitting the backtrack/unchoose step), causing subsequent sibling branches to receive corrupted shared state
Recursing to the wrong depth by off-by-one in the goal condition
quiz.explanation: Because backtracking uses shared mutable state (one path, one board, one used-array), every mutation must be reversed before the function returns. Forgetting to reverse it means the next sibling choice in the for-loop sees a modified state as if the previous choice had been made — producing wrong or incomplete results. The fix: always write the choose and unchoose steps as adjacent paired lines.

quiz.question: When should you prefer dynamic programming over backtracking for a combinatorial problem?
options: When the problem has no constraints
When you need to enumerate every valid solution rather than find just one
When subproblems overlap — the same partial state is reached via multiple paths — and you need an optimal value such as a minimum count or maximum sum
When the input size is small enough that brute force is feasible
quiz.explanation: Backtracking explores each branch independently with no caching — it is appropriate when subproblems do not overlap or when you need all solutions. Dynamic programming memoizes overlapping subproblems, reducing exponential backtracking to polynomial time when the same partial state can be reached via multiple paths. For example, coin change (minimum coins) has heavily overlapping subproblems — DP is O(n·amount); backtracking is exponential.
